analysis.one_liner: Blocks the Transportation Department from raising minimum insurance requirements for passenger bus companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2015, the bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never received a markup or vote; it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law sets minimum insurance levels (called financial responsibility requirements) that passenger bus companies must carry. This bill would lock those minimums in place, forbidding the Transportation Secretary from ever raising them, while ordering a one-year study of the current requirements to be reported to Congress. The study would examine crash and claims histories, the effect of higher limits on premiums, and whether small and school bus carriers could stay in business if limits rose.
analysis.who_benefits: Over-the-road bus companies and private school bus operators, who avoid premium increases that higher minimum liability limits would bring. Insurers and reinsurers also benefit because they avoid larger potential payouts and the capital requirements the bill itself flags.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal law so the Secretary of Transportation may not increase the minimum levels of financial responsibility for motor carriers of passengers, freezing them at the levels set by statute.

Requires the Transportation Department to conduct a comprehensive study of the current minimum requirements — covering accident and claims histories, the range of limits carriers hold, links between higher limits and fewer crashes, and effects on premiums and service availability — and report to Congress within one year.
Keeps insurance costs predictable for carriers, a concern the bill singles out for small- and medium-sized over-the-road and private school bus companies.

analysis.who_pays: People injured in bus crashes and families of those killed, who would be limited to recovering up to the frozen minimum insurance amounts even in multi-victim crashes where losses far exceed them; public programs can end up absorbing uncompensated injury costs.

drawbacks.text: Freezing the minimums leaves victims of serious bus crashes able to recover no more than the decades-old statutory minimums, even when medical bills and losses in a multi-casualty crash run far higher.
The bill's own study provisions acknowledge the other side: higher limits could raise premiums and push small, rural, and private school bus carriers out of the market, reducing service availability.
The required one-year study would delay any increase in the minimums for at least a year even if the study supported one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is lower and more predictable insurance costs for bus operators, especially small ones. The cost falls on crash victims, whose recovery would be capped at old minimums that may not cover a mass-casualty bus crash. The freeze is the bill's core effect; the study it orders is a way of examining the issue without raising anything.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on April 28, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit; no further action was taken for the rest of the 114th Congress.

The bill would have barred the Secretary of Transportation from increasing minimum financial responsibility levels for passenger carriers and required a department study with a report to Congress within one year of enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the freeze never took effect and the Transportation Secretary kept the legal authority to raise minimum insurance levels for passenger carriers — which matters most to crash victims and their families. Bus carriers and insurers also kept the status quo of unchanged minimums and premiums.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crash victims — the freeze never took effect

for.name: Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to freeze minimum financial responsibility requirements for passenger bus carriers.

against.name: Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or brought the bill to the floor; it remained in the Highways and Transit Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the record shows the sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Republicans, with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Over-the-road and private school bus carriers
industries.note: A freeze on minimum liability limits avoids premium increases the bill itself says would fall hardest on small and medium carriers. The trade-off is that victims of serious crashes could recover only up to the old minimums, so the industry's gain comes at crash victims' expense.

Higher minimums would require more underwriting capacity and capital to back larger potential payouts — issues the bill's own study section spells out. Freezing the limits keeps both the insurers' exposure and carriers' premiums where they are.
